title: Epstein–Barr virus
wiki_lead:
The Epstein–Barr virus (EBV;  EP-styne, Yiddish: [ˈɛpʃtejn]), also known as human herpesvirus 4 (HHV-4), is one of the nine known human herpesvirus types in the herpes family, and is one of the most common viruses in humans. EBV is a double-stranded DNA virus. EBV is the first identified oncogenic virus, a virus that can cause cancer. EBV establishes a permanent infection in human B cells. It is the most common cause (90% of cases) of infectious mononucleosis and is also tightly linked to many malignant diseases (cancers and autoimmune diseases). Various vaccine formulations have been tested in humans and other animals; however, none of them were able to prevent EBV infection, and no vaccine has been approved to date.
Infectious mononucleosis ("mono" or "glandular fever"), is characterized by extreme fatigue, fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes. EBV is also associated with various non-malignant, premalignant, and malignant EBV-associated lymphoproliferative diseases such as Burkitt lymphoma, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, and Hodgkin's lymphoma; non-lymphoid malignancies such as gastric cancer and nasopharyngeal carcinoma; and conditions associated with human immunodeficiency virus such as hairy leukoplakia and central nervous system lymphomas. The virus is also associated with the childhood disorders of Alice in Wonderland syndrome and acute cerebellar ataxia and, by some evidence, higher risks of developing certain autoimmune diseases, especially dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjögren's syndrome. About 200,000 cancer cases globally per year are thought to be attributable to EBV. In January 2022, a large study following 10 million active US military over 20 years suggested EBV as the leading cause of multiple sclerosis (MS), with a recent EBV infection causing a 32-fold increase in MS risk development.
Infection with EBV occurs by the oral transfer of saliva and genital secretions. Most people become infected with EBV and gain adaptive immunity. In the United States, about half of all five-year-old children and about 90% of adults have evidence of previous infection. Infants become susceptible to EBV as soon as maternal antibody protection disappears. Most children who become infected with EBV display no symptoms, or the symptoms are indistinguishable from other mild, brief illnesses of childhood. When infection occurs during adolescence or young adulthood, it causes infectious mononucleosis 35 to 50% of the time.
EBV infects B cells of the immune system and epithelial cells, and may infect T cells, NK cells, and histiocytic-dendritic cells. Once EBV's initial lytic infection is brought under control, EBV latency persists in the individual's memory B cells for the rest of their life.

grok_lead: The EpsteinâBarr virus (EBV), also known as human herpesvirus 4 (HHV-4), is a ubiquitous double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the gammaherpesvirus subfamily that primarily infects B lymphocytes and epithelial cells, establishing lifelong latency in memory B cells following initial infection. Discovered in 1964 by Michael Epstein and Yvonne Barr through electron microscopy of tumor cells from a patient with Burkitt lymphoma, EBV was the first virus identified as oncogenic in humans, infecting over 90â95% of the global adult population, often asymptomatically during childhood. It spreads primarily through saliva via close contact such as kissing or sharing utensils, though transmission can also occur via blood, semen, organ transplants, or breast milk, with the virus capable of persisting on moist surfaces. In most cases, primary EBV infection is subclinical, particularly in young children, but in adolescents and young adults, it commonly manifests as infectious mononucleosis (often called "mono"), characterized by symptoms including fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, fatigue, and an enlarged spleen or liver, typically resolving in 2â4 weeks with supportive care, though fatigue may linger for months. The virus's pathogenesis involves initial lytic replication in epithelial cells of the oropharynx, followed by B-cell infection via the CD21 receptor, leading to viral latency where it evades the immune system through restricted gene expression (e.g., EBNA1, LMP1 proteins, and EBER non-coding RNAs). Reactivation can occur in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV or post-transplant, potentially causing severe complications like lymphoproliferative disorders or hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. EBV's oncogenic potential is well-established, with latent viral proteins promoting B-cell proliferation and immune evasion, contributing to approximately 240,000â360,000 cancer cases annually worldwide; it is causally linked to Burkitt lymphoma (endemic form in Africa), Hodgkin lymphoma (30â40% of cases), nasopharyngeal carcinoma (especially in East Asia), gastric carcinoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders. Emerging evidence also implicates EBV in autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (where infected individuals face a 32-fold higher risk) and systemic lupus erythematosus (a 2025 study demonstrated EBV reprogramming of autoreactive B cells into antigen-presenting cells that drive autoimmunity), and rheumatoid arthritis, potentially through molecular mimicry and chronic immune activation. No vaccine is currently available, and diagnosis relies on serology (e.g., IgM/IgG antibodies to viral capsid antigen) or PCR for viral DNA, with treatment limited to symptom management or antivirals in severe cases.
